today: RFC 1099 is an informational document that has not been obsoleted. It remains a useful reference for understanding the range of protocols and standards developed during the 1989-1991 period of Internet development.

sections.title: The Index of 1000-1099
sections.content:
RFC 1099 is a summary document covering the 100 RFCs numbered 1000 through 1099. Published in December 1991, it works as a catalog of that specific range of the RFC series, providing concise annotations for each document.

The document organizes all 100 RFCs in numerical order, listing the author, publication date, and a brief description of each RFC's purpose and content. This makes it easy for implementors and protocol developers to navigate the RFC landscape during this period of rapid Internet growth.
sections.eli5: This is a reference book that lists all 100 rule books in a certain range and explains what each one does, so you can find the one you need.

sections.title: Key RFCs in the 1000-1099 Range
sections.content:
The range of RFCs 1000-1099 covers a diverse set of Internet protocols and standards. Notable protocols include SNMP (RFC 1098) for network management, NFS (RFC 1094) for file system access over networks, and the DNS implementation and concepts RFCs (1034 and 1035).

Telnet protocol extensions appear frequently in this range (RFCs 1079, 1080, 1091, 1096, 1097), showing the importance of remote terminal access during the late 1980s. The range also includes foundational work on SMTP extensions (RFC 1090), TCP performance improvements (RFC 1072), and various network management and monitoring systems.
sections.eli5: In these hundred documents you find rules for sending files over networks, managing Internet computers, remote terminals, email, and keeping track of network clocks.

sections.title: Coverage and Categories
sections.content:
The RFCs in this range cover protocols at multiple layers of the Internet stack: link-layer technologies like Ethernet and NetBIOS (RFCs 1042, 1001, 1002), network-layer protocols like IP options and routing (RFCs 1063, 1075), and application-layer protocols for mail, file transfer, and terminal access.

Informational and experimental documents are well represented, reflecting the RFC series' role not just in standardization but in documenting ongoing research and exploration. Some RFCs are status reports (such as RFC 1060 on Assigned Numbers), while others propose new standards (such as RFC 1095 for CMOT, the Common Management Information Protocol over TCP/IP).
sections.eli5: These documents describe rules for different parts of the Internet: how computers connect physically, how information gets routed, and what programs do.

sections.title: Historical Context
sections.content:
RFC 1099 is itself a historical document, serving as a snapshot of the Internet's standardization efforts in late 1991. Many of the protocols it summarizes are still in use today (DNS, TCP/IP, SNMP), while others have been replaced by newer versions or technologies.

The document demonstrates how the RFC series grew rapidly during this period, with over 1000 documents issued by 1991. Similar summary documents were created at RFC 1000 (covering RFCs 1-999) and at later milestones, reflecting the importance of organizing and indexing the growing library of Internet standards.
sections.eli5: This document is like a time capsule from 1991, showing which rules were important back then and helping modern people understand Internet history.
